title: Playwright, filmmaker Dustin Celestino inducted into Palanca Hall of Fame
summary: Dustin Celestino enters the Palanca Awards’ prestigious roster after winning first prize in the full-length play category five times

items: Filipino playwright and filmmaker Dustin Edward Celestino was inducted into the Hall of Fame of the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature, marking his fifth first-place honor with his play 'Kritisismo.'
Celestino has received multiple awards for his works, including second place for his play 'Seen' and various other accolades in both full-length and one-act play categories since 2017.
In addition to his theater accomplishments, Celestino has also gained recognition in film, winning Indie Movie Screenwriter of the Year and having films nominated for prestigious awards.

MANILA, Philippines – Multi-awarded Filipino playwright and filmmaker Dustin Edward Celestino — whose work has been recognized across theater, film, and literature — was inducted into the Hall of Fame of the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature on Tuesday, November 24, in Makati City.

Celestino’s full-length Filipino play, Kritisismo, earned him his fifth first-place honor, solidifying his place in the prestigious Hall of Fame of the Palanca Awards, widely regarded as the local equivalent of the Pulitzer Prize.

“It’s such an honor to be included among writers I have the greatest respect for. I’m also very happy to be part of a club that includes good friends and writing peers Mikael Co, Guelan Luarca, and Joshua So,” Celestino told Rappler. All three became Hall of Famers in 2024.

Elmer Gatchalian, a member of the board of judges for Dulang Ganap na Haba (Filipino Division), said, “We were all impressed by Kritisismo because of its dramatic structure and metatheatrical form. The full-length play stands out for its intellectual depth and sharp dialogue that examines power, class divide, and systemic oppression.”
Celestino’s other entry, Seen, won second place in the Full-Length Play category, English Division, this year.
Since 2017, Celestino has received four other Palanca first-prize awards in the full-length play category:

items: Ang Duyan ng Magiting (The Cradle of the Brave) (Filipino), 2019
Ang Pangahas na si Pepe Rodriguez (The Malevolent Pepe Rodriguez) (Filipino), 2017

blocks.text: His other Palanca wins include second prize for the full-length English play Birdie in 2024; second prize for the one-act Filipino play Elehiya in 2025; third prize for the full-length English play The Lost Filipino Patriots of America in 2022; third prize for the one-act Filipino play Fermata in 2023; and third prize for the full-length Filipino play A.Ni.Mal in 2025.

The Palanca Awards is the longest-running and most prestigious literary competition in the country. Established in 1950 and named after philanthropist and businessman Don Carlos Palanca Sr., it is sponsored by the Carlos Palanca Foundation, Inc., and is considered the gold standard in Philippine writing excellence.

In 2026, Celestino won Indie Movie Screenwriter of the Year at the 42nd PMPC Star Awards for Movies for Habang Nilalamon ng Hydra ang Kasaysayan (As Hydra Devours History). He was also nominated for Best Original Screenplay at the Luna Awards and Best Screenplay at The Eddys.
Celestino’s films Habang Nilalamon ng Hydra ang Kasaysayan and A.Ni.Mál were both nominated for Best Film at the Cinemalaya Independent Film Festival in 2025 and 2026, respectively.

In 2023, Ang Duyan ng Magiting won the Special Jury Prize at Cinemalaya, earned seven Gawad Urian nominations including Best Picture, and was one of seven films shortlisted as the Philippines’ official entry to the 96th Academy Awards.
Strange Frequencies: Taiwan Killer Hospital, which he co-wrote, competed at the 2024 Metro Manila Film Festival.
Meanwhile, Utopia won the Special Jury Prize at the 2019 Cinema One Originals Film Festival and earned Celestino nominations for Best Director and Best Screenplay.

Over seven years, Celestino staged four one-act plays at the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ Virgin Labfest (VLF): Mga Eksena sa Buhay ng Kontrabida (Scenes from the Life of an Antagonist), Doggy, Ang Munting Liwanag sa Madilim na Sulok ng Isang Serbeserya sa Maynila (The Glimmer of Light in a Dark Corner of a Beerhouse in Manila), and Fermata.
The VLF also “opened more doors” for Celestino. Those doors included writing for the series Unconditional (later streamed on Netflix) and the Viva series Di Na Muli on TV5.
Celestino was born in 1983 as the eldest of four children — three boys and a girl — to entrepreneur Edgardo Celestino and teacher and preschool owner Rocelyn Domingo.
Only English books lined their bookshelves while growing up in a two-bedroom bungalow in Quezon City, making English his first language.
“I couldn’t write in Filipino well until I was in college,” he said.
Celestino’s father — who also worked as a sales representative for pharmaceutical company Unilab — owned a chain of video rental shops, and Dustin helped curate the titles they acquired.
“I watched movies as a kid, because we had video shops. At age 11 or 12, I was already asked to curate our video shop’s library because I loved watching movies,” he recalled.

Name it — Betamax, VHS, 4+1 rental promos — he watched them all and read the covers of the VHS tapes. His father favored action flicks starring Bruce Willis, Sylvester Stallone, and Mark Dacascos, while Dustin was drawn to horror.
Celestino initially took Film at De La Salle University in Manila before shifting to Philosophy with a minor in Translation. He was part of the Malate Literary Folio from 2000 to 2004.
He began joining writing competitions in 2003 and 2004, winning four times.
“I was initially into writing English fiction,” he said. It’s a path that led him to writers’ workshops organized by Iyas, Ateneo de Manila University, and Silliman University in Dumaguete.

Celestino loved Greek mythology as a child. Aside from watching Jason and the Argonauts on Channel 9 — which “started my initial interest in mythology” — the idea of using myths as metaphors for contemporary struggles came from The Myth of Sisyphus by French philosopher and novelist Albert Camus.
What appealed to him most were the stories of mortals because they were “more relatable: Pygmalion, Icarus, Orpheus, Cassandra.”
Among his favorite foreign authors are European existentialists Camus, French philosopher and playwright Jean-Paul Sartre, and Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky.

He also admires Russian-American novelist Vladimir Nabokov, Czech-French novelist Milan Kundera, Czech writer Franz Kafka, German-Swiss poet and novelist Hermann Hesse, German novelist and poet Günter Grass, and American fictionists Philip Roth and Ernest Hemingway.
“They were very good with narratives,” he said.
Among Filipino writers, the one Celestino deems closest to them is Gregorio Brillantes.
“I think Gregorio Brillantes was the best Filipino writer,” Celestino said.
Celestino has always been a teacher, just like his mother. As a speed reader, he easily handled one of the hardest parts of the job: grading papers.

He began teaching high school at St. Scholastica’s College. Later, while he was teaching college freshmen and sophomores at Asia Pacific College, the Philippines’ shift to the K-12 curriculum left him without work in the mid-2010s.
“Walang mabigay na workload sa akin (No workload could be given to me). I was demoralized. I had to take on another job,” he shared.

He was grateful for a role as creative director, where he also handled corporate social responsibility, at an internal communications company owned by a La Salle batchmate, though he struggled with the daily commute from Fairview.
He eventually resigned to focus on writing. He devoted the first 100 days of 2017 to studying playwriting formats and reading past Palanca winners.
“I had nine entries that year,” he recalled. Both of his full-length plays (in Filipino and English) won first prize.
“I had a knack for writing screenplays,” he said. “I started writing more.” – Rappler.com
